items.abstract: <jats:p>An $n\times n$ matrix is said to have a self-interlacing spectrum if its eigenvalues $\lambda_k$, $k=1,\ldots,n$, are distributed as follows: $$   \lambda_1>-\lambda_2>\lambda_3>\cdots>(-1)^{n-1}\lambda_n>0. $$ A method for constructing sign definite matrices with self-interlacing spectrum from totally nonnegative ones is presented. This method is applied to bidiagonal and tridiagonal matrices. In particular, a result by O. Holtz on the spectrum of real symmetric anti-bidiagonal matrices with positive nonzero entries is generalized.</jats:p>
title: Self-interlacing polynomials II: Matrices with self-interlacing spectrum

items.abstract: <jats:p>We independently certify a recently posted eight-element counterexample to the real-rootedness conjecture for the support polynomial of a preorder polytope. The witness is an ordinary height-two poset. Its support polynomial is computed from all order-ideal inequalities, and non-real-rootedness is proved by a rational Laguerre-inequality certificate, with an independent Sturm-chain check. Thus the computational frontier at size eight is negative.</jats:p>
title: <p>An Eight-Element Counterexample to Real-Rootedness of Preorder Support Polynomials</p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>We present first a set of commutator relationships involving the joint quantum, semi-quantum, and number operators generated by a finite family of random variables, having finite moments of all orders, and show how these commutators can be used to recover the joint quantum operators from the semi-quantum operators. We show that any linear operator defined on an algebra of polynomials or the polynomial random variables, generated by a finite family of random variables, having finite moments of all orders, can be written uniquely as an infinite sum of compositions of the multiplication operators, generated by these random variables, and the partial derivative operators. In the terms of this sum, each multiplication operator is placed to the left side of each partial derivative operator. We provide many examples concerning the decomposition of some classic operators.</jats:p>
title: Position–momentum decomposition of linear operators defined on algebras of polynomials

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
          <jats:p>The local <jats:italic>h</jats:italic>-polynomial was introduced by Stanley as a fundamental enumerative invariant of a triangulation <jats:inline-formula>
              <jats:alternatives>
                <jats:tex-math>$$\Delta$$</jats:tex-math>
                <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                  <mml:mi>Δ</mml:mi>
                </mml:math>
              </jats:alternatives>
            </jats:inline-formula> of a simplex. This polynomial is known to have nonnegative and symmetric coefficients and is conjectured to be <jats:inline-formula>
              <jats:alternatives>
                <jats:tex-math>$$\gamma$$</jats:tex-math>
                <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                  <mml:mi>γ</mml:mi>
                </mml:math>
              </jats:alternatives>
            </jats:inline-formula>-positive when <jats:inline-formula>
              <jats:alternatives>
                <jats:tex-math>$$\Delta$$</jats:tex-math>
                <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                  <mml:mi>Δ</mml:mi>
                </mml:math>
              </jats:alternatives>
            </jats:inline-formula> is flag. This paper shows that the local <jats:italic>h</jats:italic>-polynomial has the stronger property of being real-rooted when <jats:inline-formula>
              <jats:alternatives>
                <jats:tex-math>$$\Delta$$</jats:tex-math>
                <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                  <mml:mi>Δ</mml:mi>
                </mml:math>
              </jats:alternatives>
            </jats:inline-formula> is the barycentric subdivision of an arbitrary geometric triangulation <jats:inline-formula>
              <jats:alternatives>
                <jats:tex-math>$$\Gamma$$</jats:tex-math>
                <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                  <mml:mi>Γ</mml:mi>
                </mml:math>
              </jats:alternatives>
            </jats:inline-formula> of the simplex. An analogous result for edgewise subdivisions is proven. The proofs are based on a new combinatorial formula for the local <jats:italic>h</jats:italic>-polynomial of <jats:inline-formula>
              <jats:alternatives>
                <jats:tex-math>$$\Delta$$</jats:tex-math>
                <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                  <mml:mi>Δ</mml:mi>
                </mml:math>
              </jats:alternatives>
            </jats:inline-formula>, which is valid when <jats:inline-formula>
              <jats:alternatives>
                <jats:tex-math>$$\Delta$$</jats:tex-math>
                <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                  <mml:mi>Δ</mml:mi>
                </mml:math>
              </jats:alternatives>
            </jats:inline-formula> is any uniform triangulation of <jats:inline-formula>
              <jats:alternatives>
                <jats:tex-math>$$\Gamma$$</jats:tex-math>
                <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                  <mml:mi>Γ</mml:mi>
                </mml:math>
              </jats:alternatives>
            </jats:inline-formula>. A combinatorial interpretation of the local <jats:italic>h</jats:italic>-polynomial of the second barycentric subdivision of the simplex is deduced.</jats:p>
title: Local h-polynomials, Uniform Triangulations and Real-rootedness
